tips.caveats: A key point of debate is that PURE included many participants from low- and middle-income countries; the fact that they could afford daily dairy intake suggests better socioeconomic status, which is hard to fully rule out as a confounding factor. Additionally, people with lactose intolerance can safely switch to yogurt or low-lactose milk instead of drinking regular milk.

tips.title: Eating up to one egg per day is sufficient—there is no need to eliminate eggs completely
tips.cost: No cost involved, and it takes no extra time.
tips.inPlainWords: Eating an extra half whole egg each day raises the overall mortality risk by roughly 7% in some observational models. Swapping that half egg for egg whites, fish, poultry, or nuts actually lowers the risk of death across all categories. There’s no need to cut eggs out of your diet entirely; eating up to one egg per day is completely safe.
tips.benefit: A U.S. study tracking 521,000 people found that 129,000 participants died over time. Those who ate an extra half whole egg daily had a 7% higher mortality risk (hazard ratio 1.07, 95% CI 1.06–1.08, a reliable range). Replacing that half egg with equal amounts of egg whites, poultry, fish, dairy, or nuts and legumes further reduces mortality risk, including for cardiovascular disease, cancer, and respiratory conditions. Large multi-cohort meta-analyses (such as Drouin-Chartier 2020 BMJ) confirm that consuming up to one egg per day shows no association with elevated cardiovascular risk.
tips.sources: Zhuang P, Wu F, Mao L, et al. (2021). Egg and cholesterol consumption and mortality from cardiovascular and different causes in the United States: A population-based cohort study. PLoS Medicine, 18(2), e1003508. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1003508>; Drouin-Chartier JP, et al. (2020). Egg consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease: three large prospective US cohort studies, systematic review, and updated meta-analysis. BMJ, 368, m513. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.m513>
tips.caveats: This topic remains highly debated: other long‑term studies of large populations and meta‑analyses have found no link between moderate egg consumption and mortality. The U.S. Dietary Guidelines have removed previous rigid dietary cholesterol limits. The key empirical takeaway is that eating up to one egg per day is fine; there is no scientific basis for completely eliminating eggs.

tips.title: Take baths whenever you can — don’t limit yourself to showers
tips.cost: It costs a bit more in water and electricity; each bath takes about half an hour.
tips.inPlainWords: People who bathe almost daily have roughly 28% lower risk of cardiovascular events and about 46% lower risk of brain hemorrhage compared to those who bathe fewer than twice a week.
tips.benefit: A Japanese study involving 30,000 participants followed over 19 years identified 2,097 cardiovascular events. Those who bathed almost daily showed roughly 28% lower risk of cardiovascular events than those bathing no more than twice a week (hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.62–0.84). The risk of coronary heart disease was about 35% lower (0.65, 0.45–0.94), stroke risk dropped by roughly 26% (0.74, 0.62–0.87), and brain hemorrhage risk fell by about 46% (0.54, 0.40–0.73).
tips.sources: Ukai T, Iso H, Yamagishi K, et al. (2020). Habitual tub bathing and risks of incident coronary heart disease and stroke. Heart, 106(10), 732-737. <https://doi.org/10.1136/heartjnl-2019-315752>
tips.caveats: Also, water should not be too hot and baths should not be excessively long. For older adults and those with existing cardiovascular or cerebrovascular conditions, very hot water and prolonged immersion can actually be dangerous — Japan sees many elderly deaths in bathtubs each year.

tips.title: Keep naps under 30 minutes—no longer than an hour. If you regularly need a one- or two-hour nap to get through the day, it’s time to see a doctor.
tips.cost: Free. Just set an alarm before you nap; it requires very little willpower.
tips.inPlainWords: People who nap for less than an hour show no increase in mortality or chronic disease risk, and their mental clarity actually improves. In contrast, those who nap for over an hour face roughly a 30% higher risk of coronary heart disease, and about a 20% higher risk of diabetes and obesity. So set that alarm and wake up after half an hour. If you find yourself needing a one- or two-hour nap every day just to function, that’s a clear sign you should get a medical check-up.
tips.benefit: One umbrella meta-analysis compiled data from 16 separate meta-analyses covering 244 health outcomes. An umbrella meta-analysis essentially aggregates findings from multiple existing meta-analyses. Its conclusions: individuals who nap for less than 60 minutes show no rise in overall mortality or chronic disease risk, and experience the greatest improvement in cognitive function (SMD 0.69, 95% CI 0.37–1.00—a reliable range). Naps lasting 20–30 minutes provide the biggest boost to physical performance (SMD 0.99, 95% CI 0.67–1.31). On the other hand, people who nap for over an hour face a roughly 30% higher risk of coronary heart disease, and about a 20% higher risk of diabetes and obesity. Another study used wrist-worn monitors to objectively measure naps in 1,338 adults aged 56 and older, rather than relying on self-reported questionnaires. After up to 19 years of follow-up, 926 participants had died. For every extra hour of napping, mortality risk rose by about 13% (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.04–1.23). Each additional daily nap added roughly 7% to mortality risk (HR 1.07, 95% CI 1.02–1.13). People who napped in the morning faced a roughly 30% higher risk compared to those who napped earlier in the afternoon (HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.03–1.64).
tips.sources: Du P, Li J, Hua Z, et al. (2026). Multiple Health Outcomes of Daytime Napping: A Comprehensive Umbrella Review. Public Health Reviews. <https://doi.org/10.3389/phrs.2026.1609013>; Gao C, Cai R, Zheng X, et al. (2026). Objectively Measured Daytime Napping Patterns and All-Cause Mortality in Older Adults. JAMA Network Open. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.7938>; Dashti HS et al. (2021). Genetic determinants of daytime napping and effects on cardiometabolic health. Nature Communications. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-20585-3>
tips.caveats: This topic remains somewhat controversial. Both of the aforementioned studies merely recorded nap duration without stratifying participants by health status. It’s quite possible that individuals who habitually nap for long periods already suffer from sleep apnea, anemia, hypothyroidism, depression, or other chronic conditions; thus it’s hard to isolate exactly how much of the observed mortality increase is directly attributable to napping itself. Two Mendelian randomization studies involving 453,000 and 541,000 participants respectively found only one consistent link: the more frequently a person naps, the slightly higher their blood pressure and waist circumference become. No causal effect on coronary heart disease or diabetes was detected. Consequently, you shouldn’t view “shortening naps” as a reliable strategy for lowering mortality. The recommendation to “seek medical evaluation” is essentially a Level C suggestion: if daytime fatigue is so severe that you need a lengthy nap, first examine your nighttime sleep quality; be sure to screen for sleep apnea if you snore or experience breathing pauses during sleep, and also run blood tests and thyroid function tests. For tips on how short naps can boost alertness, see Section 3, Item 11 (a 10‑minute nap in the afternoon works wonders). Information on optimal nighttime sleep duration can be found in Section 13 of this chapter (aim for seven hours per night).

tips.title: Catch up on sleep the night after a sleepless night — don’t wait until the weekend
tips.cost: No cost at all. Those extra hour or two of sleep you make up are exactly what you’d have wanted to get anyway.
tips.inPlainWords: People who get less sleep than they need and fail to make it up the following night have roughly a 15% higher risk of mortality compared to those with regular sleep patterns. Those who are severely sleep-deprived and still don’t catch up face a 42% higher risk. For people who do make up the lost sleep, no such elevated risk is observed. So, if you stay up late, go to bed early the next night.
tips.benefit: This meta-analysis involved 85,618 participants from the UK Biobank, with an average age of 61.8 years. Wrist-worn monitors tracked their daily sleep patterns over a median follow-up period of 8 years. The researchers first identified “sleep deficit nights” for each individual — nights when they got more than 2.5 hours less sleep than their personal sleep needs. The first night after such a deficit was labelled a “catch-up night”, and if participants got more sleep than required that night, it counted as a successful catch-up. Based on this, five distinct sleep patterns were identified. Compared to people with regular sleep schedules, those who were sleep-deprived and failed to catch up had a 15% higher all-cause mortality risk (HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.01–1.31). For those with a cumulative sleep deficit exceeding 3.5 hours and no catch-up, this risk rose to 42% (HR 1.42, 1.24–1.63). No significant risk elevation was found in either of the two groups that did make up their sleep deficit; for those who caught up after a moderate deficit, the HR was 1.12 (0.98–1.28). Among people who naturally get less sleep, those who were sleep-deprived and did not catch up had a 19% higher mortality risk (HR 1.19, 1.01–1.40), while those with severe sleep deficits and no catch-up faced a 38% higher risk (HR 1.38, 1.17–1.63). These findings were replicated in a separate US health survey involving 4,586 participants.
tips.sources: Li X, Zhang M, Li Z, et al. (2026). Acute sleep rebound following sleep restriction is associated with reduced mortality risk. Nature Communications. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72461-1>
tips.caveats: This is an observational study with no formal grouping of participants. It is possible that people who cannot catch up on sleep are inherently busier or in poorer health, a factor this study does not fully account for. The fact that no risk elevation was detected in the two catch-up groups only means no statistically significant difference was found; their point estimates remain above 1, so catching up on sleep does not completely eliminate all risk. Therefore, if you stay up late, you should aim to make up the lost sleep as soon as possible, but this does not give you a free pass to regularly sacrifice sleep. For the purposes of this study, “catching up on sleep” refers to getting extra sleep on the first night after a deficit, and does not include waiting until the weekend to make up the total deficit. Maintaining a regular sleep schedule where you stay up on weekdays and catch up on weekends — a pattern known as social jetlag — is itself linked to cardiovascular disease; see item 13 in this section (aim to get around 7 hours of sleep per night with consistent sleep times). The recommendation to wake up at the same time every day, including on weekends (see item 2 in section 3) does not conflict with this advice: it simply encourages you to go to bed early on the night after a sleepless night, rather than sleeping in until noon the following day.

tips.title: The longer you work night shifts, the higher your cardiovascular risk — switch if you can
tips.cost: Switching jobs or changing shifts may mean a pay cut and loss of night-shift bonuses. Job hunting takes time and determination. If you factor this into your calculations when choosing a job, the cost is effectively zero.
tips.inPlainWords: People who work night shifts develop cardiovascular disease about 13% more often than those who don’t, and cardiovascular deaths rise by roughly 27%. The longer you work nights, the worse it gets: for every additional five night shifts, cardiovascular disease risk climbs another 7%. So, when you weigh the long-term costs, it makes sense to switch shifts early on. As for cancer risk, the evidence linking night shifts to cancer is far weaker than commonly believed.
tips.benefit: A pooled analysis of 23 studies — all observational, no subgroup adjustments — shows that night-shift workers face a roughly 13% higher risk of cardiovascular events (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.10–1.16). Cardiovascular deaths rise by about 27% (RR 1.27, 1.18–1.36). Over time, each extra five night shifts adds roughly 7% to cardiovascular disease risk (RR 1.07, 1.04–1.09) and about 5% to cardiovascular mortality (RR 1.05, 1.03–1.06). Specific conditions show similar trends: coronary heart disease incidence rises by 22% (RR 1.22, 1.16–1.28) and mortality by the same amount; ischemic heart disease deaths increase by 39% (RR 1.39, 1.06–1.84); stroke mortality climbs by 49% (RR 1.49, 1.04–2.12). Stroke incidence, however, shows no significant rise (RR 1.06, 0.95–1.18).
tips.sources: Xi J, Ma W, Tao Y, et al. (2025). Association between night shift work and cardiovascular disease: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis. Frontiers in Public Health. <https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1668848>; Esposito G, Bravi F, Santucci C, et al. (2025). Night shift work and breast cancer risk in healthcare workers: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Occupational Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1093/occmed/kqaf040>; Czeisler CA, Johnson MP, Duffy JF, et al. (1990). Exposure to bright light and darkness to treat physiologic maladaptation to night work. New England Journal of Medicine, 322(18), 1253-1259. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199005033221801>
tips.caveats: All these findings come from observational studies without subgroup adjustments. Night-shift workers naturally differ from others in smoking habits, weight, and income, and full adjustments are hard to achieve. Cancer risk evidence is weaker than popular claims suggest. A pooled analysis of 12 studies involving 12,132 breast cancer cases found only a 5% higher risk among night-shift workers (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.96–1.14). Therefore, this analysis focuses on cardiovascular risk, not cancer. Not everyone must leave night shifts; you should weigh the long-term costs yourself. For those already working nights, several steps help: quit smoking (see Section 1); control blood pressure and cholesterol per medical advice (Section 12); and make up lost sleep after shifts (Section 38). Two additional strategies are worth trying: eat mainly during daylight hours, and use bright light during shifts plus near-total darkness during daytime rest to reset your circadian rhythm. Only the latter has proven effective at shifting the rhythm; ordinary indoor lighting leaves it unchanged even after six night shifts. Bright light at 7,000–12,000 lux combined with near-total darkness restores it in four days. Crucially, all three measures — bright night-time light, strict daytime darkness, and sunglasses on the way home — must be used together; skipping any one negates the effect. Both strategies affect metabolism and sleep only; no trials have shown they lower cardiovascular risk. On days off, returning to a daytime routine resets the rhythm again. Full numbers and sources are set out in the research notes for this chapter.

tips.title: Buy packaged cooking oil that carries an FSSAI licence number; be wary of loose, unlabelled ghani oil of unknown origin
tips.cost: The price difference is modest if you buy branded packaged oil from a shop; a litre of mustard or groundnut oil costs what it costs, and the packaging is part of the price. What it takes is reading the label: the pack must show an FSSAI licence or registration number, a batch number and a best-before date. The real difficulty is persuading older family members who swear by the oil pressed at a local ghani.
tips.inPlainWords: When peanuts and oilseed go damp and mouldy they produce aflatoxin, a confirmed human carcinogen that damages the liver, and cold-pressing does not remove it. Loose oil sold from a drum or from a shop’s own press, with no label and no licence number, is where the risk sits: it escapes the routine sampling that packaged oil goes through. Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, anyone manufacturing, processing, packing or selling cooking oil must hold an FSSAI licence or registration, and packaged oil has to meet the contaminant limits in the FSS (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Regulations, 2011. A licence number is not a guarantee of purity, but it is what makes the seller traceable and a bad batch recallable.
tips.benefit: Aflatoxin is a Group 1 carcinogen in the International Agency for Research on Cancer classification, meaning it is established to cause cancer in humans, liver cancer above all. Measurements of home-pressed peanut oil from small producers in Guangzhou between 2010 and 2022 found a median aflatoxin B1 concentration of 1.29 μg/kg, with half of all samples between 0.12 and 6.58 μg/kg. After local rules for small producers took effect, levels fell by 2.865 μg/kg at once and by a further 2.593 μg/kg each year, and the share of local residents with abnormal liver function fell by 35% (PR 0.650, 95% CI 0.469-0.902). A cohort of 1,611 pregnant women found that 81.7% ate home-pressed peanut oil, and that those who did had a nearly 90% higher risk of a low-birth-weight baby (adjusted OR 1.9, 95% CI 1.1-3.2) and an 80% higher risk of preterm delivery (adjusted OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.1-3.0). These are studies of small oil-pressers elsewhere; they are cited because the product, the mould and the toxin are the same wherever oil is pressed without testing, and published Indian data on aflatoxin in ghani oil is thin.

tips.caveats: Both studies are observational, with no randomised control group. The first tracked liver function test results, not liver cancer or deaths. The median aflatoxin level in the home-pressed oil was below the 20 μg/kg limit that Guangzhou food-safety regulators applied at the time (GB 2761-2017, a standard that is not Indian law), so the risk comes from long-term daily consumption and from occasional batches far above the median - which is exactly why a traceable, tested supply matters more than one good sample. Indian contaminant limits apply to all cooking oil sold, licensed or not; what the licence adds is inspection and the ability to trace a bad batch back to a producer. Buying packaged oil does not make it healthy in quantity: it is still fat, and how much you use matters more than the brand. The people who benefit are you and everyone who eats from the same kitchen.

tips.title: Replacing lard and butter with vegetable oils for cooking: you don’t need to switch oils for health reasons, nor should you expect flaxseed oil to protect your heart
tips.cost: It doesn’t cost much extra. Vegetable oils are already the main choice in most households; the real challenge is breaking the habit of using lard or butter for stir‑frying and seasoning.
tips.inPlainWords: Cutting back on saturated fats like lard and butter and switching to vegetable oils lowers the risk of heart disease and stroke by roughly 17%. However, overall mortality shows no change. There is no evidence that swapping between soybean oil, corn oil, or canola oil makes any difference. Even consuming large amounts of flaxseed oil does not appear to reduce heart disease risk.
tips.benefit: A Cochrane review analyzed 15 randomized trials involving 56,675 participants, each followed for at least two years. Reducing saturated fat intake lowered the combined incidence of cardiovascular events by about 17% (RR 0.83, 0.70–0.98). Total mortality remained virtually unchanged (RR 0.96, 0.90–1.03) as did cardiovascular death (RR 0.95, 0.80–1.12). No significant difference was found between replacing saturated fats with polyunsaturated fats (the main component of soybean and corn oils) or with carbohydrates. Data on replacing them with monounsaturated fats (dominant in canola and olive oils) are too limited to draw conclusions. Another Cochrane review of 19 trials with 6,461 participants found that higher intake of omega‑6 fatty acids (linoleic acid) had no effect on overall mortality (RR 1.00, 0.88–1.12) or cardiovascular events (RR 0.97, 0.81–1.15). A third review of 86 trials involving 162,796 participants showed that increased consumption of plant‑derived omega‑3 fatty acids (found in flaxseed oil and perilla oil) had virtually no impact on overall mortality (RR 1.01, 0.84–1.20) or coronary events (RR 1.00, 0.82–1.22).

tips.caveats: Controversy: Some argue that the high omega‑6 content in soybean and corn oils promotes inflammation, so they recommend limiting or replacing these oils. The aforementioned omega‑6 study found no harmful effects, though the authors rated the evidence quality as low. The magnitude of benefit—a 17% reduction in cardiovascular events—is considered moderate, while overall mortality shows no change. Regardless of the oil type, portion control is essential; dietary guidelines suggest a daily limit of 25–30 grams of cooking oil per person.

tips.title: Turn on the range hood while stir-frying and deep-frying, from the moment you light the stove until the cooking is done.
tips.cost: For households already equipped with a range hood, the extra expense is just a bit more on the electricity bill. For those without one, buying and installing a unit costs roughly ₹5,000–₹25,000, and a chimney that vents outside costs more than a recirculating model. The real challenge is remembering to turn it on every time you cook — don’t turn it off just because it makes noise.
tips.inPlainWords: Among non-smoking women, those who do most of the cooking at home and rarely or never use a range hood face roughly twice the risk of developing lung cancer compared with those who use one regularly. Living in a kitchen with poor ventilation also raises this risk by about 50%, with the effect being most pronounced among households that burn coal.
tips.benefit: Thirteen case-control studies among non-smoking women were pooled for analysis. In these studies, researchers compared lung cancer patients with healthy individuals, asking about past cooking habits. Overall, exposure to cooking fumes was linked to a 1.74-fold increase in lung cancer risk (95% CI 1.57–1.94). Four of these studies specifically looked at women who used no range hood while cooking; their risk was 2.11 times higher (95% CI 1.54–2.89). One Taiwanese study compared 1,302 non-smoking women with lung cancer to 1,302 healthy women, focusing on those with at least ten years of cooking experience. Women who used their range hood for more than two-thirds of those years had roughly half the risk of developing lung cancer compared to those who used it for less than a third of the time (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.32–0.76). A Shanghai-based prospective study followed 71,000 non-smoking women from 1996 to 2009, identifying 429 cases of lung cancer. Women who reported living in a poorly ventilated kitchen had a 49% higher risk of lung cancer (HR 1.49, 95% CI 1.15–1.95). Those who had burned coal in such kitchens for over 20 years faced a 2.03-fold increase in risk (HR 2.03, 95% CI 1.35–3.05). No significant difference in risk was found between women who did and did not burn coal at all (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.84–1.26), nor between those using different types of cooking oil.

International Journal of Cancer, 136(3), 632-638. <https://doi.org/10.1002/ijc.29020>; Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>. The published titles of the three studies name the country or city the study populations came from and are omitted here; each DOI resolves to the full record.
tips.caveats: There is some debate regarding these findings: the evidence supporting regular range hood use comes largely from case-control studies done in Shanghai and in Taiwan, and no Indian study has measured the effect here. Since participants recall past habits after being diagnosed with lung cancer, they may underreport how often they used their range hoods, potentially inflating the observed risk figures. The Shanghai study showed the greatest risk increase among households burning coal in poorly ventilated kitchens; it did not provide separate risk estimates for households using only gas. For this reason, the overall evidence grade is set at B, while the benefit is considered substantial based on the roughly twofold difference in risk. Women who regularly do the cooking at home are the primary beneficiaries of this measure; see Item 29 of this chapter for more information on avoiding coal and wood for cooking and heating.

tips.title: If severe perimenopausal hot flushes and night sweats disrupt your daily life, seek clinical evaluation for hormone replacement therapy; do not endure in silence, self-medicate, or use it to prevent heart disease
tips.cost: Requires a consultation at a gynecology or menopause specialty clinic. The clinician evaluates medical history and contraindications before prescribing appropriate regimens. Regular follow-up checkups are mandatory during therapy. The primary hurdle is overcoming unfounded fears that "all hormones immediately cause cancer," while avoiding over-the-counter anti-aging marketing claims.
tips.inPlainWords: Menopausal hormone therapy reduces the frequency of moderate-to-severe hot flushes by roughly 75% compared to placebo. However, it carries a small excess risk of breast cancer, deep vein thrombosis, and stroke—amounting to roughly 8 additional cases per 10,000 women annually for each condition. For women initiating therapy between ages 50 and 59, all-cause mortality does not increase. It should never be prescribed to prevent heart disease or dementia.
tips.benefit: A Cochrane systematic review of 24 randomized controlled trials involving 3,329 women compared oral hormone therapy with placebo: women receiving hormone therapy experienced an approximate 75% reduction in weekly hot flushes compared to placebo (95% CI 64.3–82.3), alongside a significant reduction in symptom severity (OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.07–0.23). Women in placebo arms also experienced a 57.7% reduction in symptoms, demonstrating why controlled comparisons are critical. Adverse event risk profiles were established by the landmark U.S. Women's Health Initiative (WHI) randomized trial involving 16,608 postmenopausal women aged 50–79 with an intact uterus receiving combined estrogen plus progestin (mean follow-up 5.2 years): coronary heart disease increased by 29% (HR 1.29, 95% CI 1.02–1.63), invasive breast cancer increased by 26% (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.00–1.59), stroke increased by 41% (HR 1.41, 95% CI 1.07–1.85), and pulmonary embolism increased 2.13-fold (HR 2.13, 95% CI 1.39–3.25). In absolute numbers, this corresponds to approximately 7 additional cases of coronary disease, 8 additional strokes, 8 additional pulmonary embolisms, and 8 additional invasive breast cancers per 10,000 women per year, alongside 6 fewer colorectal cancers and 5 fewer hip fractures. Conversely, for women with prior hysterectomy receiving estrogen alone, cumulative 13-year follow-up showed a 21% reduction in breast cancer incidence (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65–0.97). Across 18 years of cumulative follow-up for both trials combined, all-cause mortality did not differ between hormone therapy and placebo (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.94–1.03). In age-stratified analyses, women initiating therapy between ages 50 and 59 experienced a 31% reduction in all-cause mortality during the intervention phase (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.51–0.94), whereas older cohorts showed no mortality benefit (ages 60–69: HR 1.04; ages 70–79: HR 1.13); at 18-year post-intervention follow-up, the mortality difference in the 50–59 group was no longer statistically significant (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.79–1.01). A 2017 Cochrane review focusing on women aged 50–59 noted venous thromboembolism as the only significantly elevated risk with combined therapy, with an absolute incidence under 1 in 500. In women aged 65 and older on combined therapy, dementia diagnoses rose from 9 to 11–30 cases per 1,000 women over 4 years. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) 2022 recommendation explicitly advises against using hormone therapy for the primary prevention of chronic conditions in postmenopausal persons (Grade D recommendation), finding no net clinical benefit.

The mortality reduction observed in the 50–59 age bracket was a subgroup finding that attenuated over 18 years, meaning hormone therapy cannot be characterized as a life-extending longevity intervention. Contraindications generally include previous breast cancer, active or prior thromboembolism, high cardiovascular risk, and severe obesity, requiring individual clinical assessment. Women with an intact uterus must pair estrogen with a progestin to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer; estrogen alone is reserved for individuals with prior hysterectomy. While hormone therapy reduces osteoporotic fractures, it is reserved for symptom control or cases where first-line osteoporosis drugs cannot be tolerated (see Chapter 1, Item 39 and 40). Benefit magnitude is rated High based on the 75% reduction in severe vasomotor symptoms. Primary beneficiaries are yourself, your mother, or your partner.

tips.title: If you already plan to adopt a dog, count daily dog walking toward your physical activity goals, but do not acquire a dog solely expecting to extend lifespan
tips.cost: Dog ownership represents a substantial, ongoing financial commitment covering food, vaccinations, parasite prevention, veterinary care, licensing, and grooming across the animal's entire lifespan. It demands daily dedicated time for walking and care arrangements during travel. The difficulty lies in mandatory daily adherence that cannot be paused when inconvenient.
tips.inPlainWords: Observational studies show that dog owners have an average 24% lower risk of all-cause mortality, with even stronger associations among individuals living alone following a heart attack or stroke. However, once studies fully adjust for socioeconomic status, physical activity, and baseline health, large cohorts in the UK and Norway found zero difference in mortality, and owning cats shows no association. Do not get a dog purely as a health intervention; if you already have or want one, leverage daily walks toward your step count.
tips.benefit: A meta-analysis pooling 10 prospective cohort studies comprising 3.84 million participants with a mean follow-up of 10.1 years reported that dog owners had a 24% lower risk of all-cause mortality (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.67–0.86) and a 31% lower risk of cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.67–0.71). Among individuals with prior coronary disease, owning a dog was associated with a 65% lower mortality risk (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.17–0.69); however, the authors noted this pooled estimate did not adjust for key lifestyle confounders. A nationwide Swedish registry study of 3.43 million adults adjusting for income, marital status, and education found that among single-person households, dog ownership was associated with a 33% lower mortality risk (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.65–0.69), and an 11% lower risk in multi-person households (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.87–0.91). Among Swedish post-myocardial infarction patients, single dog owners experienced a 33% lower risk of death (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.61–0.75), and post-stroke patients had a 27% lower risk (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.66–0.80). Conversely, an analysis of 6 British health survey cohorts comprising 59,352 adults followed for a mean of 11.5 years found that after full multivariable adjustment, dog ownership showed no association with all-cause mortality (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.98–1.09) or cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.07, 95% CI 0.96–1.18). A Norwegian HUNT study cohort followed for a median of 18.5 years similarly revealed virtually identical mortality rates between dog owners and non-owners (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.91–1.09), with dog owners exhibiting no higher physical activity than peers. An analysis of 34,202 Swedish twins with comprehensive lifestyle data failed to replicate the association between dog ownership and lower cardiovascular disease or death. An Australian cohort of 15,735 adults found an initial 23% lower mortality risk (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.59–0.99) that was partially mediated by greater walking volume; owning cats, birds, or fish showed no correlation with mortality. An American Heart Association (AHA) scientific statement concluded that pet ownership, particularly dog ownership, "may be reasonable" for cardiovascular risk reduction (Class IIb, Level of Evidence B recommendation—the weakest recommendation grade), and explicitly advised against adopting, rescuing, or purchasing a pet primarily to reduce cardiovascular risk.

tips.caveats: Controversy: All available evidence consists of observational registries without randomized assignment, making reverse causality and healthy-user bias prominent (people capable of caring for a dog are often healthier, wealthier, and more mobile). When studies comprehensively adjust for lifestyle factors, the apparent survival advantage largely disappears. In another Swedish registry, dog owners actually initiated antihypertensive and lipid-lowering therapies at slightly higher rates, indicating that any real benefit is not mediated by lower baseline blood pressure or cholesterol. The practical takeaway is straightforward: if you already own a dog or plan to adopt one, integrate mandatory daily walks toward your daily step target (7,000–8,000 steps per day, as described in Chapter 2, Item 11). Statutory leash laws, mandatory rabies vaccination, and third-party bite liability are detailed in Chapter 8, Item 30. Techniques for elderly family members to grip leashes properly and avoid catastrophic falls are covered in Chapter 17, Item 10. Benefit magnitude is categorized as High based on the unadjusted 24% relative reduction, though residual confounding is substantial. Primary beneficiary is yourself.

tips.title: If diagnosed with prediabetes (elevated blood glucose below diabetes threshold), delay progression through dietary caloric restriction, weight loss, and increased physical activity; retest glucose every six months
tips.cost: Zero financial cost; eating less saves a little money. Accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity (such as brisk walking) per week, averaging ~20 minutes daily. Reduce daily caloric intake by 400 to 500 kcal compared to baseline. The primary difficulty is lifelong consistency and preventing weight regain once lost. Retest blood glucose every six months (fasting blood glucose costs about ₹80–₹200 at a private lab, less at a government hospital).
tips.inPlainWords: For individuals with elevated blood glucose who have not yet reached the diagnostic threshold for diabetes, eating less, moving more, and losing a modest amount of weight reduces the risk of progressing to full diabetes by 30% to 60%. However, similar trials in the US and Finland did not observe statistically significant differences in all-cause mortality.
tips.benefit: The Da Qing Diabetes Prevention Study was a clinic-randomized trial conducted in Da Qing, Heilongjiang Province, enrolling 577 adults with impaired glucose tolerance (a form of prediabetes) assigned to control or three 6-year intervention arms: diet alone, exercise alone, or combined diet plus exercise. Six-year cumulative diabetes incidence was 67.7% in controls versus 43.8% (diet), 41.1% (exercise), and 46.0% (combined). After adjusting for baseline BMI and fasting glucose, diabetes risk fell by 31%, 46%, and 42% respectively, with comparable reductions across lean and overweight subgroups (BMI cutoff 25). At 23-year follow-up, the combined intervention group had 41% lower cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.36–0.96), 29% lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.51–0.99), and 45% lower diabetes incidence (HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.40–0.76). At 30-year follow-up, median onset of diabetes was delayed by 3.96 years; composite cardiovascular events were 26% lower (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.59–0.92), severe microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) were 35% lower (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.45–0.95), cardiovascular mortality was 33% lower (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48–0.94), all-cause mortality was 26% lower (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.61–0.89), and mean survival was prolonged by 1.44 years (95% CI 0.20–2.68). In the U.S. Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) trial of 3,234 adults with prediabetes, the intensive lifestyle arm targeted at least 7% weight loss and at least 150 minutes a week physical activity: over a mean 2.8-year period, diabetes incidence fell by 58% (95% CI 48%–66%) compared to placebo, while metformin reduced incidence by 31% (95% CI 17%–43%). Over 15-year follow-up, lifestyle intervention maintained a 27% diabetes reduction (HR 0.73), though between-group divergence narrowed. At 21-year median follow-up, all-cause mortality (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.81–1.28) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.77–1.81) showed no significant differences compared to controls. In the Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study (DPS) of 522 overweight adults with impaired glucose tolerance, lifestyle intervention reduced 4-year cumulative diabetes incidence by 58% (11% vs 23%), maintaining a 43% reduction at median 7-year follow-up; at 10.6 years, all-cause mortality showed no significant difference (HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.21–1.58).

tips.caveats: Controverted regarding mortality endpoints. All three major trials conclusively demonstrate reduced and delayed diabetes incidence; however, a statistically significant reduction in all-cause mortality was observed only in the Da Qing trial (which enrolled 577 participants, originally powered for diabetes incidence rather than mortality). Participants in the U.S. and Finnish trials had baseline BMI >30, whereas Da Qing participants averaged BMI 25.7, with notable benefits even in participants with minimal weight loss, suggesting dietary composition and physical movement drive benefits independently of mass reduction alone. Start by eliminating sugary drinks (Chapter 2, Item 7). Activity targets are detailed in Chapter 2, Item 11 (7,000–8,000 steps daily). BMI targets are outlined in Chapter 2, Item 32 (BMI 20–25). Screening thresholds are described in Chapter 1, Item 8 (fasting blood glucose screening). Metformin also delays diabetes onset but is less effective than lifestyle modification; its initiation requires medical prescription. Benefit magnitude is categorized as High based on the 26% reduction in all-cause mortality in the Da Qing trial. Primary beneficiary is yourself.

tips.title: If peanuts, corn, tree nuts, rice or flour go mouldy, throw out the whole packet rather than picking out the visibly spoiled pieces; spit out a bitter nut at once
tips.cost: Throwing away a spoiled packet of peanuts, dry fruit or grain costs a few tens to a couple of hundred rupees, more for cashews and pistachios. Store dry goods cool, dry and ventilated, buy smaller packets, and do not stockpile before a festival. The hard part is the reluctance to waste food, strongest in the oldest person in the kitchen.
tips.inPlainWords: Mouldy peanuts and maize produce aflatoxins, potent chemical carcinogens that cause liver cancer. In a long-term prospective cohort of 18,244 middle-aged men in Shanghai, men with detectable aflatoxin in their urine had about 3.4 times the risk of liver cancer of men without it, and men who also carried hepatitis B had about 59 times the risk of men with neither. Aflatoxins survive boiling, roasting and frying.
tips.benefit: Aflatoxins are Group 1 human carcinogens in the International Agency for Research on Cancer classification, causing hepatocellular carcinoma. They grow most readily on peanuts, maize and tree nuts, and they are heat-stable: ordinary boiling, baking and frying do not destroy them. A prospective cohort enrolled 18,244 middle-aged men in Shanghai from 1986, collected urine at baseline and followed them for roughly 70,000 person-years, during which 55 liver cancers occurred. Comparing 50 cases with 267 matched controls, men with detectable urinary aflatoxin biomarkers had 3.4 times the odds of liver cancer (relative risk 3.4, 95% CI 1.1-10.0). A positive hepatitis B surface antigen test carried 7.3-fold risk (RR 7.3, 95% CI 2.2-24.4). Men positive for both had 59.4-fold risk (RR 59.4, 95% CI 16.6-212.0) against men negative for both. In earlier multivariable analyses adjusted for hepatitis B, smoking, alcohol and education, aflatoxin exposure still carried a 3.8-fold elevation (95% CI 1.2-12.2). In Qidong, Jiangsu Province, a historically high-incidence liver cancer area, the staple shifted in the 1980s from locally stored maize to rice brought in from the regional market: median serum aflatoxin-albumin adducts fell from 19.3 pg/mg in 1989 to undetectable (<0.5 pg/mg) by 2009, and liver cancer mortality in cohorts born after the shift fell by more than half, before infant hepatitis B vaccination was widespread. The researchers attributed about 65% of the decline to lower dietary aflatoxin exposure, with 83% of the averted deaths among chronic hepatitis B carriers. Global risk models put aflatoxin’s carcinogenic potency roughly 30-fold higher in hepatitis B carriers than in non-carriers.

tips.caveats: The Shanghai figures measure the association between internal biomarker exposure and liver cancer; no trial randomises households to throw out or keep mouldy food. Baseline urine was collected only once in that cohort. In Qidong, serum adducts became undetectable by 2009 following the dietary shift. The magnitude of benefit is rated Moderate because modern household grain storage is vastly better than the historical rural baseline, so exposure today is lower. Why the whole packet: public health agencies advise that once opened nuts or grain show a musty smell or visible mould, invisible fungal threads and spores have spread through the container, and shaking the packet disperses them further. The US Department of Agriculture’s food safety guidance is to discard peanut butter, legumes, nuts, cooked pasta and bread that show any mould; only firm low-moisture vegetables such as cabbage, capsicum or carrot can be salvaged by cutting at least 2.5 cm around the spot. If you bite a nut that tastes bitter or mouldy, spit it out and rinse your mouth. Hepatitis B carriers face this risk multiplied; if you have never checked your hepatitis B status, see Chapter 1, Item 14. Avoiding unrefined small-workshop peanut oil is Chapter 2, Item 40. Unspoiled nuts remain worth eating, as Chapter 2, Item 22 sets out. The people who benefit are you and everyone who shares the meal.

tips.title: Avoid eating raw or drunken freshwater fish and shrimp (including freshwater sashimi, raw fish porridge, and drunken prawns); if you have eaten them regularly, test for liver flukes and take prescribed praziquantel
tips.cost: Avoiding raw freshwater fish costs nothing; the difficulty is breaking long-standing regional dietary customs and declining dishes during social dinners. If you have eaten freshwater sashimi in the past, a hospital stool microscopy test for fluke eggs costs a few hundred rupees. If infected, physician-prescribed praziquantel is taken over 1 to 2 days.
tips.inPlainWords: The liver fluke Clonorchis sinensis is an established biological carcinogen: infected people face roughly 4 to 5 times the risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer) compared to uninfected peers. Condiments like vinegar, alcohol, and wasabi do not reliably kill liver fluke larvae. Once diagnosed, a two-day course of prescription anthelmintic medication cures over 90% of infections.
tips.benefit: Clonorchis sinensis was evaluated in 2009 by the WHO International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) and classified as a Group 1 biological carcinogen causing cholangiocarcinoma (upgraded from Group 2A in 1994). A comprehensive meta-analysis of risk factors found that liver fluke infection was associated with a 4.8-fold increase in cholangiocarcinoma risk (relative risk 4.8, 95% CI 2.8–8.4), surpassing the relative risks of hepatitis B (2.6) and hepatitis C (1.8). Another systematic review pooling 36 studies reported odds ratios for cholangiocarcinoma of 4.37 (95% CI 2.84–6.72) in case-control studies and a relative risk of 10.43 (95% CI 2.90–37.47) in cohort studies. Infection was also associated with marked elevations in cholangitis and cholecystitis (RR 7.80), gallstones (RR 2.42), and hepatocellular carcinoma (OR 4.69). Effective destruction requires continuous freezing below -20°C for at least 7 days, or cooking until internal food temperature exceeds 70°C for over 10 minutes. Marinated and cold-smoked freshwater fish also remain infectious. For medical treatment, a 2022 network meta-analysis of 26 trials comprising 3,340 participants demonstrated that the WHO-recommended oral praziquantel regimen (25 mg/kg three times daily for 2 days) achieved an estimated cure rate of 98.5% (95% CI 85.4%–99.9%) against Clonorchis sinensis.

tips.caveats: Risk estimates derive from observational case-control and prospective registries rather than randomized controlled trials. Cholangiocarcinoma is relatively rare in the absolute population, meaning that despite elevated relative risk, absolute risk remains modest for people outside the regions where raw freshwater fish is everyday food. Grade B is assigned. Adult liver flukes can survive inside the human bile duct system for 20 to 30 years; mild chronic infections often produce zero symptoms, so individuals with regular raw freshwater fish exposure should not wait for symptoms before testing. Stool microscopy for ova provides definitive diagnosis; liver ultrasound, CT, and serology are supportive. Praziquantel dosing must be determined by a physician based on body weight and infection severity; in areas where cysticercosis is co-endemic, detailed medical history is required before high-dose therapy to avoid neurological adverse events. Cured individuals can be reinfected if they continue eating raw freshwater fish. Always use separate knives and chopping boards for raw seafood versus cooked foods. Marine sashimi carries different parasites (such as Anisakis larvae). Pregnant women, young children, and older adults should strictly avoid raw seafood. Hepatitis B and C also induce liver malignancy, detailed in Chapter 1, Item 14, and Chapter 1, Item 45. Primary beneficiaries are yourself and dining companions.
